To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
infants as young as 4 months of age are able to detect the direction of another person's attention and are able to follow it.
infants as young as 4–5 months of age show signs of affective self-other consciousness, and that these signs are already present at the end of their first year of life.

(1) infants' attention is directed to the mother's gaze in the first month of life and to the mother's mouth in the second month; (2) infants' attention to the mother's face is accompanied by an affective self–other experience; (3) infants' attention in the second month is directed to the object of the mother's attention, and to the mother as well; (4) the infant's attention to the object of attention is accompanied by a positive affective
In summary, our research is concerned with
the origins of social cognition, and how it relates to self-consciousness, affect and emotion.
the emergence of self and other awareness in infancy and the role of joint attention in this process.
the development of the self, other, and self-other relations in the early years of life, and the implications of this for the development of social cognition and social relations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-conscious affects in infancy are not only the first form of self-consciousness, but also the first form of other-consciousness.
the self is the object of attention from birth, and that the self-other distinction is not a conceptual one, but an affective one. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
the infant is not only conscious of the self, but also conscious of other people's consciousness of the self.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not born into a world of self–other consciousness, but rather we are born into a world in which self–other consciousness is possible.
the self is not a unitary concept but rather a complex of interrelated and overlapping concepts.
we have shown how the infant's self-other conscious affects, as the first object, are the foundation for the infant's later conceptual self–other representations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the infant's self–other consciousness, as expressed in mutual gaze, can be understood as an affective experience, not just a cognitive one.
infants' affective engagement with others, even in the first months, is a form of consciousness of self and other.
the self is not a late development but rather a fundamental aspect of the earliest forms of self-other consciousness.
